title: Periodic Table Adventure (Chemistry)
welcome_lead: Today you'll explore the periodic table — its history, its layout and its famous families of elements.
meta_desc: GCSE Chemistry Periodic Table foundations — Mendeleev's gaps, groups and periods, alkali metals, halogens and noble gases.
final_note: You learned how Mendeleev built the table, how groups and periods work, and the key features of groups 0, 1 and 7.

walkthroughs.body_html:
In 1869 Mendeleev arranged the known elements by mass and properties.

His big idea: leave gaps for elements not yet discovered, and predict their properties. When gallium and germanium were found, they matched his predictions almost perfectly.

Today's table is ordered by atomic number, not mass.

Columns are groups. Elements in the same group have the same number of outer electrons and behave similarly.

Rows are periods. Elements in the same period have the same number of electron shells. Metals sit on the left, non-metals on the right.

Group 1 — alkali metals: lithium, sodium, potassium. Soft, very reactive, react with water to give hydrogen and an alkali.

Group 7 — halogens: fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine. Coloured non-metals that form salts. Group 0 — noble gases: helium, neon, argon. Almost no reactions.

mcqs.q: What did Mendeleev do that was new?
options: He used atomic number
He left gaps for undiscovered elements
He invented isotopes
He grouped only metals

mcqs.q: Why does first ionisation energy generally increase across a period?
options: Atoms get bigger across a period, making electrons easier to add but harder to remove.
Isotopes are atoms of different elements with the same mass.
Nuclear charge increases while shielding stays roughly constant, so electrons are held more tightly.
Atoms across a period have more shells, pulling electrons closer.

mcqs.q: What is different between two isotopes of the same element?
options: Isotopes are atoms of different elements with the same mass.
Isotopes have different numbers of electrons, which is why their mass differs.
Benzene cannot react with electrophiles at all.
They have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.

mcqs.q: Why does benzene undergo electrophilic SUBSTITUTION but alkenes undergo electrophilic ADDITION?
options: Atoms across a period have more shells, pulling electrons closer.
Benzene cannot react with electrophiles at all.
Substitution preserves benzene's stable delocalised pi system; addition would destroy aromaticity at a large energetic cost.
Benzene reacts the same way as alkenes — by addition across one of its double bonds.
